newsitem.title: CHINA: New China state debt market to hurt local mkts.
newsitem.headline: New China state debt market to hurt local mkts.

text.p: China's plans to set up a unified national state debt market this year will diminish the role of regional exchanges and trading centres, in particular the Shanghai stock exchange, analysts said on Tuesday.
The central government wants to centralise state debt trading by the end of 1997 in order to give it more control over the market and to reduce irregularities, they said.

"The central government, especially the central bank and the Finance Ministry, want to use the market to gain more direct involvement in the financial markets and to strengthen control over the financial industry," said a state debt analyst.
"It also aimed at reducing the role of regional exchanges," the analyst, working with a major Chinese brokerage, said.
Regional centres currently trading the debt have objected to the proposal, fearing a loss of income and influence.
The Shanghai exchange, which handles 90 percent of all state debt publicly traded in China, is most exposed, analysts said.

"All the trading volume will be excluded from regional exchanges and trading centres once the market goes into full operation," said one state debt analyst with a major Chinese brokerage. "This will significantly reduce their role."
An official with the Shanghai stock exchange declined to comment on the issue.
"Trading is expected to continue as normal on all the exchanges and securities trading centres around the nation but through the computerised network of the new market," said a state debt trader.
"This will remove an important source of commission for the regional markets, and also reduce their liquidity sharply."
China revived the financial markets in the early 1990s and allowed the stock exchanges in Shanghai and Shenzhen to do the bulk of the state debt trading.
But the new exchange will shift the balance of power back to Beijing and alter the balance between the two bourses in favour of Shenzhen, analysts said.
In 1996, state debt accounted for 63 percent of the turnover on the Shanghai exchange, while it made up only 4.5 percent of Shenzhen's business.
Excluding state debt, stock turnover in Shanghai in 1996 came to 911.4 billion yuan ($109.8 billion), significantly behind Shenzhen's 1.22 trillion yuan.

As a preparation for the new market, the People's Bank of China, the Finance Ministry and six other shareholders established and registered the China Government Securities Depository Trust and Clearing Co in December last year.
In another preparatory move, the People's Bank of China, the central bank, recently banned major state banks from trading on the current state debt secondary markets.

Industry sources said Beijing had not decided how to deal with existing state debt positions in the banks' hands, but that a possible outlet was to allow the banks to trade them through the new market.

"I believe the ban is just a temporary measure to curb widespread irregularities on the state debt secondary market, in particular margin trading," said a trader. "It is very possible that the ban will be lifted on the new market."
